_note: What an operator wears, as clothing rather than as kit (src/game/outfit.ts). The kit in gear.json is the hard stuff strapped on top: plates, a helmet, a mask. This is the clothes under it, and it is what makes one figure a soldier and another a man in a t-shirt. Every piece is a shell along a bone, and every bone in this rig points along its own +y with a measured length (thigh 0.400 m, calf 0.429, upper arm 0.274, forearm 0.273), so a sleeve is a tube from 0 to a fraction of that length and nothing has to be rigged or weighted. Sizes are metres on a figure 1.8 m tall; colours are hex strings.

fit._note: the body's own thicknesses, which the clothes sit just outside of
fit._profile: how thick the body is along each bone: metres from the bone's own axis, six samples from the start of the bone to its end. Measured off the model by tools/checks/body.ts, which checks these numbers against it. A limb is not a cylinder, and a garment built on one number is either inside the body at the wide end (the arm is 84 mm at the shoulder) or a barrel at the narrow one (61 mm at the elbow).
fit._body: the body up the spine bone, band by band, the way the limbs are measured along theirs: six bands from `from` to `to` of the bone's length, each with the body's width, its depth and where its middle sits front to back. Measured off the model by tools/checks/body.ts. The spine bone leans back, so the middle drifts from +20 mm at the hips to -69 mm at the shoulders; one box on that axis is too wide at the waist, too shallow at the chest and 90 mm out at the collar, which is where the body used to stand out of its own jacket.
fit._gone: torso and torsoAt were one box and one offset for the whole body, typed in by eye. They are replaced by `body` above, measured band by band, and nothing reads them any more.

_builds: How heavy-set a figure is. The body underneath is one mannequin and one set of hit boxes, and that does not change: what changes is how thick the CLOTHES on it are and how wide across the shoulders they sit, which is what reads as build at any distance. Keeping the hit boxes identical is the point rather than a shortcut: a game where a bigger-looking character is easier to hit is a game where nobody picks them.
_pieces: each piece: the bone it hangs on, how far along that bone it starts and ends as a fraction of the bone's length, and how much thicker than the body it is

a piece with no kind is a shell along its bone, turned along the body's own profile. 'rags' hangs strips off one, which is what breaks a silhouette rather than colouring it; 'stripe' runs a band down the outside of one, which is what a tracksuit is.
_head: the things that cover a face, in the head bone's rest frame: x its right, y up it, z in front of it. A wrap is a shell round the skull with a tail down the back; goggles are two round lenses on a strap; a full mask covers the whole face, where the gas mask in gear.json covers the nose and mouth.

head._mxHelmet: a motocross helmet: a shell round the whole skull, a dark visor band where the eyes are, a chin bar across the jaw and a peak over the brow. It covers a face on its own, which is why the set that wears it needs nothing else on its own. Every number is against the head measured off the model by tools/checks/body.ts: 173 mm across, -9 to 256 mm up the Head bone, and a face that reaches 106 mm forward of it.

_sets: The outfits: what each wears, and in what colours. `cloth` is the main garment, `trim` the second colour, `boots` the footwear. An operator names one of these (src/game/operators.ts), and the kit in gear.json goes on top of it.
_realSets: A set with `character` is a real asset: a whole clothed figure, mesh and textures, from Quaternius's CC0 Modular Character Outfits (public/models/outfits, tools/fetch-characters.ts). The game swaps the figure's own mesh for it and builds no garments of its own, because its clothes ARE the mesh. Everything without `character` is built in code out of shells on bones, which is cheap, fits any rig and looks like what it is.
